questions.q: Identify the grammatical voice used in the line "The arch was built too low" and name the tense.
questions.a: The line uses passive voice in the simple past tense ("was built"). A wrong answer (e.g., "active voice" or "past perfect") reveals the student cannot distinguish passive construction or identify tense in a poetic context where the subject ("The arch") receives the action.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the poet uses the passive voice repeatedly in the first half of the poem (e.g., "was built", "were arranged", "was led", "must be hanged").
questions.a: The passive voice shifts focus from the doer (the King, the workmen) to the action and its recipient, creating a bureaucratic, impersonal tone that mimics official records — this reinforces the satire of a justice system that follows procedure without logic. A wrong answer (e.g., "to make it sound poetic") shows the student misses the link between grammatical choice and satirical purpose.

questions.q: Rewrite the reported speech in the stanza beginning "The chief of builders was led out. / He passed the King. He gave a shout, / 'O King, it was the workmen's fault'" into direct speech, preserving the original meaning and verse rhythm.
questions.a: Direct speech version: The chief of builders shouted, "O King, the workmen are at fault!" Steps: 1) Identify reporting verb ("gave a shout") and reported clause. 2) Change pronoun "it" to "the workmen" and verb "was" to "are" for present relevance. 3) Adjust punctuation to verse. A wrong answer that keeps "was" or misses the vocative "O King" shows inability to convert reported to direct speech in a poetic register.

questions.q: Compare the sentence structure of the King's decree "I do ordain that you shall be / Hanged" with the idiot's reply "A melon." What grammatical contrast does this create, and how does it serve the poem's ending?
questions.a: The King's decree is a complex periodic sentence with a main clause ("I do ordain") and a subordinate noun clause ("that you shall be hanged"), using the archaic emphatic "do ordain" and modal "shall" for legal force. The idiot's reply is a noun phrase fragment ("A melon") — no verb, no clause. This contrast grammatically enacts the shift from pseudo-legal verbosity to absurd minimalism, underscoring the collapse of reasoned governance. A wrong answer that only notes "one is long, one is short" misses the structural and functional analysis.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the poet's use of the archaic verb form "hanged" (instead of "hung") throughout the poem. Does it strengthen or weaken the satirical tone? Justify.
questions.a: "Hanged" is the correct legal term for execution by hanging, while "hung" is used for objects. Seth's consistent use of "hanged" mimics precise legal language, heightening the mock-formal tone — the state treats execution as a procedural correctness. This strengthens the satire because the bureaucracy cares about the right word while killing an innocent man. A wrong answer claiming "hanged/hung doesn't matter" shows ignorance of register and legal diction.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza in the style of the poem (rhyming couplets, mock-legal tone) that uses at least two passive constructions and one archaic verb (e.g., "ordain", "proclaim", "edify") to describe a modern bureaucratic absurdity (e.g., a pothole repair, a lost file).
questions.a:
Example:
The file was lost in the office deep,
The clerk was told to never sleep.
The officer did ordain with sigh:
"Refile the form before you die."
Criteria: rhyming couplets, two passives ("was lost", "was told"), one archaic verb ("ordain"), satirical modern context. A poor answer lacking passives or archaic verb shows inability to apply grammatical features creatively.
